paras: The whipping of Si Liddell and Jones was the flogging of two Black men by a crowd near Glory, Texas, in August 1905, after an improvised tribunal convicted them of remarks about a young white woman. Both men were whipped and ordered to leave the community. Papers outside Texas treated the case as a curiosity: one called it a "double lynching" averted by a "Kangaroo Court," while a wire version stressed that Black residents had helped punish the men.

Glory lay twenty miles west of Clarksville by most copies of a Clarksville dispatch (one says east); the St. Louis Republic spelled it "Gloria." The dispatch said two young men were charged with making "defamatory remarks about the daughter of a prominent white farmer," while the Republic's Houston correspondent wrote that Liddell "had made improper remarks to a young white woman."

In the Clarksville version, the two men were arrested on Saturday morning, August 19, and kept chained in a building through the day. That night they were taken to a meadow half a mile east of the village, where about 700 residents, "composed equally of blacks and whites," had gathered. A committee of ten, five white and five Black, was appointed to try them, and after several witnesses were examined the men were found guilty. One was sentenced to forty lashes and the other to twenty-five, and the five Black committee members carried out the whipping, each giving eight lashes to the first man and five to the second. The men were then released and given five days to leave the community.

The St. Louis Republic's special from Houston, dated August 20, gave a different and fuller account. It said a mob of 200 men "quietly formed at Gloria," seized Liddell and Jones, and took them to a pasture, where ropes were placed around their necks for a double lynching. When some counseled moderation, the mob instead set up a tribunal with a judge, a sheriff, a jury of twelve and attorneys, naming the man who had warned it "to go slow" to defend the two men.

By the Republic's account, the jury found them guilty and fixed the punishment at whipping rather than death: 100 lashes for Liddell and twenty-five for Jones. Ten mob leaders named as deputies by the mob's "sheriff" each gave Liddell, tied to a tree, ten lashes with ropes and straps, and Jones was whipped the same way. The men, "badly used up," were warned to depart and were believed far from town by midnight. It added that several Black men among the mob took an active part in the trial.
No report of arrests or legal action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage, nor any report of whether the two men left as ordered.

The story reached white papers on August 21 in two independent versions. The wire ran in the Alexandria Gazette as "Negroes Whipped," in the Providence News as "Whipped Two Negroes, Convicted of Slander," and in the New Haven Union and the New York Sun under "Slanderers Lashed," with the subhead "They Were Negroes, But Negroes Help to Punish Them." These versions called the men "culprits" and "slanderers" and treated the crowd's verdict as settled.

The Republic headlined its version "Mob Conducts Mock Trial; Double Lynching Is Averted," calling the tribunal a "Kangaroo Court" whose "deputies" carried out the sentence, though its text shows they were mob members. A week later the Durango Semi-Weekly Herald drew an editorial lesson: a mob "about to hang a negro in Texas" had given him a trial and found him deserving only of a lashing, a course it said "might be commended to other anti-negro mobs." All of the coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report of the episode was located.

The two versions differ on the crowd (200 men or 700 residents), the tribunal (a jury of twelve or a mixed committee of ten), the first man's sentence (100 lashes or forty) and who used the whip (deputized mob leaders or the Black committee members). Only the Republic reported the ropes; the wire mentions no threat to kill. The Republic also dated the seizure August 20, while the Clarksville dispatch, filed nearer the scene, put it on Saturday, August 19.

reader.title: Whipping of Si Liddell and Jones
bases: A public crowd seized two Black men, tried them before an improvised tribunal, flogged them and ordered them out of the community (A1, A2, A3); one version adds that ropes were first put around their necks (A1), but no one was killed and no secret band is described.

Two independent reports, the St. Louis Republic's Houston special (A1, A2) and the Clarksville wire (A3, A5, A7), agree that two Black men near Glory were tried by a crowd for remarks about a young white woman, whipped and told to leave, though they differ on numbers and details.

accounts.gist: The men were arrested Saturday morning, chained in a building, and tried that night before 700 Black and white residents by a committee of five white and five Black men; the Black members gave 40 and 25 lashes and the men were given five days to leave.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic special from Houston
accounts.gist: A mob of 200 seized Liddell and Jones, put ropes around their necks, then held a mock trial with judge, sheriff, jury and attorneys; ten deputized mob leaders whipped Liddell 100 lashes and Jones 25, and the men were warned to depart.

framing.detail: The Clarksville wire called the men 'culprits' and 'slanderers', treated the guilty finding as settled, and headlined that 'Negroes Help to Punish Them'.

The St. Louis Republic ran a stacked headline, 'Mob Conducts Mock Trial; Double Lynching Is Averted', describing a 'Kangaroo Court' as a curiosity managed 'with as much decorum as a regular tribunal'.
The Durango Semi-Weekly Herald commended a trial and lashing to 'other anti-negro mobs' as more productive than hanging.
